name: EGCG

lead: EGCG is the most abundant catechin in green tea, sold as a concentrated extract in fat-burner and pre-workout products. Users take it for a small extra calorie burn and slightly lower body fat.

It may modestly raise energy expenditure and fat oxidation by prolonging noradrenaline signalling and may reduce fat absorption in the gut. Trials and meta-analyses of green tea catechins show small effects on weight and fat mass, varying with caffeine intake and baseline habits. Some users speculate about muscle effects via myostatin, an idea based on lab findings.

paras: It is taken as a capsule or extract, often before workouts and combined with caffeine-based thermogenics and L-carnitine. Brewed green tea is another route.

Concentrated extracts, especially on an empty stomach, have been linked to rare liver injury; in 2018 the European Food Safety Authority said 800 mg or more daily from supplements could raise liver-damage risk. The FDA issued warning letters to EGCG supplement makers between 2008 and 2017. It can reduce iron absorption and interact with some drugs. Brewed tea is considered safe.

chain: Green tea catechin raises metabolism slightly
angle.text: EGCG is a green tea extract taken as a fat burner, where a slightly higher metabolism adds a small extra calorie burn and slightly lower body fat. Studies show small thermogenic effects with mixed results; the muscle-building talk comes from lab findings and users.

lead: Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG, epigallocatechin-3-gallate) is the most abundant catechin in tea, an ester of epigallocatechin and gallic acid. It occurs at high levels in dried green tea leaves (about 7,380 mg per 100 g), white tea and, in smaller amounts, black tea, and is sold in concentrated form in many dietary supplements.[1]

In physique and fat-loss circles it is taken as a fat-burner or pre-workout ingredient, often alongside caffeine-based thermogenics and L-carnitine, and some forum users have speculated about effects on myostatin.[2][3][4][5] Wikipedia describes EGCG as heavily studied in basic research with various biological effects in the laboratory, while the human evidence for specific health claims is limited.[1]

Safety is a documented concern at high doses: the European Food Safety Authority stated in 2018 that a daily intake of 800 mg or more of EGCG from supplements could raise the risk of liver damage, and the US FDA issued warning letters to EGCG supplement makers between 2008 and 2017 over disease claims and quality control.[1][6]

paras: EGCG extracts are marketed for fat loss and metabolic support. T Nation posters suggest taking an EGCG extract before training, sometimes with a thermogenic fat-burner, or using it during structured diets such as the Velocity Diet, and a supplement maker's page lists it among products for cellular, cardiovascular and metabolic health.[2][3][4][7]

Laboratory and clinical interest covers cancer prevention, inflammation, neurodegeneration and skin conditions, among others. Reviews summarise catechin effects on health, cancer and inflammation, and trials have examined topical EGCG in vitiligo and green tea extract for preventing colorectal adenomas.[8][9][10][11][12]

A 2016 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (NCT02147041) tested high-dose green tea extract providing 856.8 mg of EGCG daily in 102 women with central obesity, with outcomes including weight, lipid profile and obesity-related hormone peptides.[13] A 2016 review cited by Wikipedia found that daily doses of 107 to 856 mg over four to 14 weeks produced a small reduction in LDL cholesterol, whereas a 2011 EFSA analysis could not establish a cause-and-effect link between tea catechins and normal LDL levels.[1]

A 2018 randomized trial examined polyphenol supplementation and intramuscular apoptotic signalling after acute resistance exercise.[14] A 2022 randomized trial tested green tea extract for preventing colorectal adenomas, and a 2021 trial tested topical EGCG in vitiligo.[9][10] Registered trials cover esophageal cancer symptoms, radiotherapy-related esophagitis, colorectal cancer chemoprevention, Down syndrome cognition and foetal alcohol syndrome, among others; an insulin-response trial in obesity and hypertension was registered but withdrawn.[15][16][17][18]
No published trial of EGCG in healthy lifters has established an effect on myostatin or muscle mass.

Wikipedia reports that oral EGCG is poorly absorbed even at intakes equivalent to 8 to 16 cups of green tea, which can cause nausea or heartburn.[1] A 2018 review concluded that excessive intake may cause liver toxicity, and EFSA concluded in 2018 that 800 mg or more per day could increase the risk of liver damage; the same sources describe 338 mg per day as considered safe in capsule form and 704 mg per day as safe when consumed as tea.[1][6] A United States Pharmacopeia review also examined the hepatotoxicity of green tea extracts, and a 2018 review examined the safety of green tea and extract consumption in adults.[19][20]
A T Nation poster notes that tea-derived products can cause morning nausea on an empty stomach.[21]

After oral intake EGCG levels in blood peak within about 1.7 hours, with an absorbed plasma half-life of around 5 hours and most unchanged EGCG excreted in urine within about 8 hours. Methylated metabolites have longer half-lives and reach 8 to 25 times the plasma levels of unmetabolised EGCG.[1]

In laboratory work EGCG has been reported to inhibit NF-kappa-B-dependent inflammatory signalling, inhibit DNA methyltransferase in cancer cell lines, remodel amyloid and alpha-synuclein fibrils, scavenge radicals, and activate AMPK, among many other effects whose relevance to people taking oral supplements is uncertain given low absorption.[22][23][24][25][26]

Between 2008 and 2017 the FDA sent several warning letters to makers of EGCG supplements, mostly for promoting them as treating or preventing diseases, which classifies them as unapproved new drugs, and one for inadequate quality assurance and labelling.[1] EGCG is sold under many supplement brands, and a T Nation thread discusses discontinued products from a supplement maker.[27]

lore.intro: In bodybuilding forums EGCG is treated as a fat-burner and general-health supplement, and a 2007-2008 thread speculated about myostatin inhibition.[2][3][4][28]
